newsitem.title: SURINAM: Dutch insist Bouterse arrest warrant not political.
newsitem.headline: Dutch insist Bouterse arrest warrant not political.

text.p: Dutch officials rejected on Wednesday Suriname's charge that an arrest warrant for former military strongman Desi Bouterse was politically motivated.
Meanwhile, analysts warned that the growing battle between the Netherlands and its former colony could threaten the Surinamese government's fragile political alliance.
Suriname's President Jules Wijdenbosch accused the Netherlands on Tuesday of calling for Bouterse's arrest for alleged involvement in drug trafficking as a political ploy.

"But we insist that it is a purely judicial affair, that our Attorney General is autonomous," A Dutch embassy spokesman said on Wednesday. The Hague will respond next week to a Surinamese request to revoke the arrest warrant, he said.
Although he holds no public office, Bouterse was recently made special adviser to Wijdenbosch and is widely seen as the real power in the small South American country.
"He might not be the president, but he is the de facto leader of the country," George Findlay, editor-in-chief of De West newspaper said.

While Bouterse's National Democratic Party (NDP) is pressing for a hard-line response to the Dutch legal proceedings, other coalition members are nervous of wrecking close, but already tense, bilateral relations.
"The other coalition members are not totally anti- Netherlands, so this whole matter could destroy the coalition and bring down the government," Findlay said.
Bouterse, who seized power in 1980 and 1990 coups and ran a military government through most of the 1980s, defiantly rejected Dutch charges that he was involved in drug smuggling.
"If they're looking for trouble, they've come to the right place," he told a political rally on Monday night.
The burly 51-year-old ex-army sergeant, however, told supporters they should refrain from attacking the Dutch embassy and the 25,000 Dutch nationals in the country.
Political analysts interpreted Bouterse's comments as a thinly-disguised threat. "Why else would he say that?" said one analyst, who asked not to be named.
Government officials and supporters said the investigation into Bouterse's links to drug trafficking were motivated by a desire to destabilize Wijdenbosch's administration.
"History has shown that the Netherlands always has a political score to settle with political leaders who want to make something of Suriname," congressman Frank Playfair said.
Opposition parties have called for Bouterse to resign as presidential advisor and warned the government not to jeopardize Suriname's relationship with the Netherlands.
With a population of just over 400,000, Suriname depends heavily on development aid from the Netherlands and has close commercial and family ties. More than 250,000 Surinamese live there.

Allegations of Bouterse's involvement in drug trafficking have appeared in the Dutch press periodically for more than 10 years, but it is only recently that authorities have confirmed that they were pursuing a criminal investigation against him.
The head of the Dutch public prosecution service said earlier this year that he expected to bring charges against Bouterse within several months.
Although not a drugs producer, Suriname is a major trans-shipment point for Colombian cocaine bound for western Europe.
